\chapter{This One and That One}
\label{ch:mr-ha-to}
\hlchaptermodality{69}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can point at something near or far in the right gender, and I can talk about a third person.}

From cold: the two-by-three grid of pointing words, the fact that the front carries distance while the ending carries the noun's gender, and the far row doing double duty as he, she and it.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[hā / hī / he]{\mr{हा} / \mr{ही} / \mr{हे} (hā / hī / he) — \textquotedblleft{}this\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:MR-C69-ha}



\begin{quote}
Three nouns, three genders. \textbf{\mr{मित्र}} is masculine, \textbf{\mr{खोली}} is feminine, \textbf{\mr{घर}} is neuter. Say all three before you turn the page.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{हा}, \mr{ही}, \mr{हे}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{हा}} \emph{hā} · \textbf{\mr{ही}} \emph{hī} · \textbf{\mr{हे}} \emph{he} — \textbf{this}
\end{quote}

English has one word for this. Marathi has three, and \textbf{which one you use is decided by the noun, not by you}:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\mr{हा} \mr{मित्र}} \emph{hā mitra} & this friend \\
\textbf{\mr{ही} \mr{खोली}} \emph{hī khoolī} & this room \\
\textbf{\mr{हे} \mr{घर}} \emph{he ghar} & this house \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

You have made this choice before. \textbf{\mr{माझा}} and \textbf{\mr{माझी}} split the same way, on the same two endings — \textbf{-\mr{आ}} for a masculine noun, \textbf{-\mr{ई}} for a feminine one. So the first two rows are a habit you already have, pointed at a new word.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: it goes in front, and it never stands alone here}]
\textbf{\mr{हा}} sits \textbf{before} its noun — \emph{hā mitra}, never \emph{mitra hā}. That is the same slot \textbf{\mr{माझा}} and \textbf{\mr{डावा}} take, so the front of a Marathi noun is becoming a place you know: the words that describe it queue up there.

And because the ending is chosen by the noun, \textbf{the word tells you the gender of anything that follows it.} Meet a noun you have never read, with \textbf{\mr{ही}} in front of it, and you already know one true thing about it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{hā mitra}, \emph{hī khoolī}, \emph{he ghar}
  \item which of the three endings matches \textbf{\mr{माझा}}
  \item where the word sits — before the noun or after it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you say \emph{this room}? (\emph{\textbf{\mr{ही} \mr{खोली}}}.) Who chooses between \mr{हा}, \mr{ही} and \mr{हे} — you, or the noun? (\textbf{The noun}.) And where does the word go? (\textbf{In front}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[to / tī / te]{\mr{तो} / \mr{ती} / \mr{ते} (to / tī / te) — \textquotedblleft{}that\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:MR-C69-to}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{this house}, \emph{this room}, \emph{this friend}. Keep the three endings in your ear; only their front is about to change.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{तो}, \mr{ती}, \mr{ते}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{तो}} \emph{to} · \textbf{\mr{ती}} \emph{tī} · \textbf{\mr{ते}} \emph{te} — \textbf{that}
\end{quote}

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{near} & \textbf{far} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\mr{हा}} \mr{मित्र} & \textbf{\mr{तो}} \mr{मित्र} \\
\textbf{\mr{ही}} \mr{खोली} & \textbf{\mr{ती}} \mr{खोली} \\
\textbf{\mr{हे}} \mr{घर} & \textbf{\mr{ते}} \mr{घर} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{Only the first letter moved.} \mr{ह}- became \mr{त}-, and the three endings did not budge, because they were never about distance — they were about the noun.

That is the whole of the second lesson. You learned six words by learning four.

\begin{culture}
One warning worth having before you meet \textbf{\mr{ते}} on a page.

You have already read \textbf{\mr{ते}} in this book, and it was \textbf{not} this word. In \textbf{\mr{एक} \mr{ते} \mr{पाच}} — \emph{ek te pāc} — it means \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}one to five\textquotedblright{}}, a stretch between two numbers. Same three letters, different job.

Nothing in the shape tells them apart. \textbf{What tells them apart is what sits beside it}: a noun after it makes it \emph{that}; two numbers around it make it \emph{to}. Marathi will do this to you again, and the habit of reading the neighbours rather than the word alone is what gets you through it.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{to mitra}, \emph{tī khoolī}, \emph{te ghar}
  \item each near word and its far partner, as a pair
  \item the other job \textbf{\mr{ते}} does, and how you would tell which is which
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you say \emph{that house}? (\emph{\textbf{\mr{ते} \mr{घर}}}.) What is the only difference between \emph{this room} and \emph{that room}? (\textbf{The first letter}.) And what else can \textbf{\mr{ते}} mean? (\emph{\textbf{To}}, between two numbers.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hā · to]{\mr{हा} · \mr{तो} — two rows, and what the far one is really for}

\label{lesson:MR-C69-dem-system}



\begin{quote}
Say the six words, near row first, in the order masculine, feminine, neuter.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: two rows, not three}]
\textbf{Marathi points in two directions and stops.} \textbf{\mr{ह}-} is here; \textbf{\mr{त}-} is not here. There is no third word for \emph{that one over there, further away}.

Spanish needs three — \emph{este}, \emph{ese}, \emph{aquel} — and English is unstable about it, keeping \emph{yonder} alive only in corners. Marathi draws the line \textbf{once}, between what is at hand and what is not, and everything not at hand shares one row.

That is fewer words to learn and one fewer decision to make while speaking.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the far row is also he, she and it}]
Here is the part that matters most, and it is not about pointing at all.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{तो}} — \emph{that} — is also \textbf{he}. \textbf{\mr{ती}} — \emph{that} — is also \textbf{she}. \textbf{\mr{ते}} — \emph{that} — is also \textbf{it}.
\end{quote}

Marathi does not keep a separate set of third-person pronouns. \textbf{It reuses the far row.} Whoever is not you and not the person you are speaking to is, by default, \emph{the one over there}.

So this chapter did more than teach pointing:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\mr{मी}} & I \\
\textbf{\mr{तू}} / \textbf{\mr{तुम्ही}} & you \\
\textbf{\mr{तो}} / \textbf{\mr{ती}} / \textbf{\mr{ते}} & he / she / it \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{That is the whole set of people a sentence can be about}, and until now you had the first two rows and not the third.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item how many directions Marathi points in
  \item \emph{to}, and then both things it can mean
  \item the three rows of people — I, you, and the third
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many directions does Marathi point in? (\textbf{Two} — here and not here.) How do you say \emph{she}? (\emph{\textbf{\mr{ती}}} — the same word as \emph{that}.) And does Marathi have a separate word for \emph{he}? (\textbf{No} — it reuses the far row.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hā ani to]{(this one and that one) — from cold}

\label{lesson:MR-R69-dem-recall}



\begin{quote}
Close the lessons before this one. Draw the grid from memory: two rows, three columns.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: four letters, six words}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{masculine} & \textbf{feminine} \\
\midrule
\textbf{near} & \textbf{\mr{हा}} & \textbf{\mr{ही}} \\
\textbf{far} & \textbf{\mr{तो}} & \textbf{\mr{ती}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The neuter completes each row — \textbf{\mr{हे}} and \textbf{\mr{ते}} — and the grid is done.

\textbf{Two fronts and three endings make six words.} The front carries the distance and is yours to choose; the ending carries the gender and is the noun's. Neither decision touches the other, which is why six words cost you four.

All six sit \textbf{in front} of their noun, in the slot \mr{माझा} and \mr{डावा} already use.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Pointing, and \textbf{the third person}.

\textbf{\mr{तो}}, \textbf{\mr{ती}} and \textbf{\mr{ते}} are \emph{he}, \emph{she} and \emph{it} as well as \emph{that}. Before this chapter a Marathi sentence could be about you or about the person you were speaking to, and about nobody else. Now it can be about anyone.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the near row, then the far row
  \item \emph{this room} and \emph{that room}
  \item \emph{he}, \emph{she}, \emph{it} — without looking
  \item which part of each word the noun decided
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many pointing rows does Marathi have? (\textbf{Two}.) Say \emph{that room}. (\emph{\textbf{\mr{ती} \mr{खोली}}}.) And what else do \mr{तो}, \mr{ती} and \mr{ते} do? (\textbf{They are \emph{he}, \emph{she} and \emph{it}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
